catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shi-koku:
Shi-koku, one of Japan's four great islands, covers 7,009 square miles without its smaller dependencies and held 3,199,500 people by the census of 1909. Its name means Four Kingdoms, since from ancient times it was split into Awa in the east, Sanuki in the northeast, Tyo in the northwest, and Tosa in the south. At the Restoration of 1868 the provinces were renamed, and the island now forms the prefectures of Tokushima, Kagawa, Ehime, and Kochi.

Density runs to 176 people per square mile, rising to 418 in Kagawa, higher than in any other prefecture of Japan. The climate is mild and healthy, and Tosa alone in the empire grows two rice crops a year. The land is very mountainous, reaching 6,480 feet at Tshizuchi-Yama in Ehime. People crowd the seacoast. Schools of many kinds abound, but there is no university. Buddhism and Shinto both decline as religious indifference grows among the young.
